what: MakeMyTrip is India’s largest online travel company. It sells flights, hotels, holiday packages, bus tickets (through redBus) and train tickets through its MakeMyTrip and Goibibo apps.
customers: Indian travellers booking domestic and international trips, and companies booking travel for employees.
money: Commissions and margins on hotel stays and holiday packages.
redBus tickets, trains, cabs and ads.
moat: The leading brand in Indian online travel, with by far the largest share of hotel bookings and a wide range of travel products.
risks: Shareholders’ equity is negative ($-91M) after the company raised debt to buy back Trip.com’s stake in 2025.
Debt of $1.47B, partly convertible, means dilution if the shares rise.
The trailing P/E of 178 is distorted by charges and taxes; adjusted earnings are higher.
Competition from Google, airlines’ own sites and other online agencies.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $304M in fiscal 2022 to $1.04B in fiscal 2026.
Cash of $809M and steady free cash flow of about $160–180M a year.
Indian travel demand is growing fast as incomes rise.
Ten analysts average a target near $68, about 41% above the price.
watch: Hotel booking growth and how the company handles its new debt.
view: MakeMyTrip is the best way to own the growth of Indian travel, and the business has delivered: revenue has more than tripled in four years and it generates real cash. The trailing P/E of 178 is misleading; on forward earnings it is about 22.

The 2025 buyback of Trip.com’s stake changed the balance sheet. It is now financed with debt and convertibles, which leaves equity negative and creates future dilution. The trade-off was removing an overhang from a large seller.

This turns on whether Indian travel keeps growing at double-digit rates. I think it will. At about 22 times forward earnings, the shares look reasonably priced for that growth, with the leverage as the main thing to watch.
bull: Indian travel grows rapidly for years and MakeMyTrip keeps its leading share.
bear: Growth slows, competition intensifies and the convertibles dilute shareholders.
